extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics and scholars of allegory/John Bunyan
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging allegorical prose (especially Bunyan's 'Holy War' and 'Pilgrim's Progress'): suitability of subject, artistic completeness, handling of theological problems, characterization, realism of spiritual struggle, and rhetorical/vivid qualities. Focus is on how allegory functions as art and as a vehicle for doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic completeness / natural ending
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of art the drama should have a natural end: 'the fair beginning, the perils, the struggles, and the final victory of good.' At that point 'the curtain ought to fall.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful allegorical drama should present a coherent beginning–middle–end with resolved conflict; leaving the narrative artificially open or unfinished weakens its artistic effect. The 'Holy War' is criticized because its theological situation makes a natural artistic closing difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making allegory expose theological contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting unresolved theological difficulties within an allegory emphasises problems rather than soothing them: such emphasis 'serves only to revive Man Friday's question' and may puzzle the reader and 'his faith wavers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theological mysteries remain unresolved, an allegory risks undermining the reader's confidence; allegorical treatment should not unnecessarily foreground dilemmas that art cannot satisfactorily resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cross-question an allegory too minutely
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory 'must not be cross-questioned too minutely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should accept some symbolic ambiguity and not insist on overly literal or exhaustive explanations of every allegorical element; excessive literalism diminishes imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject matter for allegory (individual vs collective)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Holy War' is an unfit subject for allegorical treatment because the struggle is left undecided; by contrast 'Pilgrim's Progress' is 'no less perfectly adapted for it' because it represents 'the efforts of a single soul after holiness' and has a natural termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects with an inherent, narratively resolvable arc for allegory—individual spiritual journeys fit best; representing the unfinished struggle of humanity as a whole can frustrate the demands of dramatic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intention and freedom (writing for oneself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan wrote 'Pilgrim's Progress' 'for his own entertainment' and 'without the thought... of what the world would say about it.' This inward authorship contributed to its authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work produced primarily from personal conviction or private need (rather than to please public fashion) often attains greater sincerity and artistic power; avoid shaping allegory chiefly for external approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and human truthfulness of the protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pilgrim, though in Puritan dress, is 'a genuine man' whose experience is 'so truly human' that Christians of every persuasion and even some non-believers can identify with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical protagonists should embody experiences and emotions of broad human sympathy so that the work transcends narrow sectarian limits and speaks to a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and picturesque opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong opening lines (e.g., 'As I walked through the wilderness of this world I lighted on a certain place...') are praised as 'picturesque and vivid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A memorable, vividly-imagined opening quickly establishes tone and engages the reader; effective allegory often begins with striking, image-rich narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic depiction of ongoing spiritual struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion is not an end of struggle: 'The path of duty is unfortunately not strewed with flowers at all. The primrose road leads to the other place.' Persistence and recurring temptations must be depicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray spiritual progress as an ongoing, often difficult process with relapses and trials; depicting only immediate triumphs will ring false to lived experience and weaken psychological credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of didactic episodes/resting-places to teach distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes such as the 'Interpreter's House' function to 'learn to distinguish... passion and patience' and to show 'the action of grace on the heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-crafted episodic scenes (resting-places) allow the allegory to instruct—each should illuminate a moral or spiritual distinction without becoming merely abstract exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as embodiments of virtues and vices (typology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures like Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Mr. Legality, Mr. Talkative, Formalist, Hypocrisy, and others clearly embody specific moral failings or virtues (e.g., Mr. Talkative's religion 'lieth in his tongue').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognisable types to personify particular vices or graces; such typology helps readers grasp moral lessons, but should avoid reducing characters to caricature that destroys psychological plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in portrayal of doubt and inner conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan 'places' skeptical states of mind directly in his pilgrim's path (Valley of the Shadow of Death), and 'it speaks well for Bunyan's honesty' that such misgivings are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict internal doubts authentically; inclusion of sincere skepticism strengthens credibility and moral seriousness of the allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain doctrinal role-boundaries and internal theological coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Emmanuel's address to Conscience prescribes limits: 'Thou must confine thyself to the teaching of moral virtues... but thou must not attempt to presume to be a revealer of those high and supernatural mysteries... In all high and supernatural things, thou must go to him for information and knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical structures should respect internal theological/hierarchical roles (e.g., who can reveal mysteries vs. who teaches moral duties) so that doctrinal representation remains coherent and internally consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between theological truth and artistic demands
rubrics_metrics.description: The text distinguishes 'for purposes of art' and 'for purposes of truth'—art may demand a different treatment (e.g., closure) than theological truth strictly allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theological realities and artistic form conflict, the writer must balance fidelity to doctrine with the necessities of narrative art; rigidly insisting on theological completeness can harm artistic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory can and should reflect social/political realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan uses Mansoul as emblematic of 'fashionable London' and notes how commerce and abundance ('the Devil's wares') can corrupt and make the castle a warehouse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory may incorporate social, economic, and political observation to illuminate moral dangers; use specific contemporary social detail to increase resonance and critical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing affect allegory's reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pilgrim's Progress was 'composed exactly at the time when it was possible for such a book to come into being'—allegory flourishes when a religion moves from living faith to a form governed by language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cultural and historical context when composing or assessing allegory: a work's power depends partly on how well it addresses the prevailing spiritual and social mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-didacticism—preserve narrative interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Though didactic, the Pilgrim's path is relieved 'by adventures and humorous conversations' and vivid incidents; Bunyan's liveliness prevents the book from being merely a doctrinal tract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix instruction with incident, humour, and character interplay so moral teaching does not overwhelm storytelling; narrative variety sustains reader engagement.
